stem: Which statement best describes the main purpose of containment during incident response?

options.text: Limit how far the threat can spread and how much damage it can do
Remove all of the attacker tools and persistence from every affected system
Return the affected services to normal operation for everyday users
Identify the person responsible so that legal action can begin

explanation: Containment stops the spread and limits impact while the investigation continues. Removing attacker tools is eradication, returning services to users is recovery, and attribution is not a goal of containment.

stem: A responder must collect evidence from a running compromised host. Which source is the most volatile and should be collected first?

options.text: A disk image taken from the mounted system drive of the compromised host
The contents of memory and the list of running processes
Archived backup media stored in an offsite vault
Printed copies of last month's firewall reports

explanation: Memory and process state disappear at power-off or reboot, so they come first in the order of volatility. Disk contents persist longer, and backup media and printed reports are the least volatile.

stem: What does a chain of custody record document for a piece of digital evidence?

options.text: The market value of the device holding the evidence
The vendor, version and license details of the forensic software that was used
Who handled the evidence, when, and why, from collection to storage
The list of vulnerabilities found on the device at collection

explanation: A chain of custody tracks every person who held or moved the evidence, with dates and reasons, so it stays defensible. Device value, tool details and vulnerability findings may appear in other records but do not show custody.

stem: An analyst computes a cryptographic hash of a forensic image immediately after acquiring it. What is the main purpose of that hash?

options.text: To compress the image so that it takes less storage space
To encrypt the image so that only the case team can open it
To identify which operating system was installed on the source drive
To prove later that the image has not changed in any way since the moment it was collected

explanation: Recomputing the hash later, before use or transfer, returns the same value if the image is unchanged. A hash does not compress or encrypt data, and it says nothing about the installed operating system.

stem: Which activity belongs to the eradication phase of incident response?

options.text: Removing a persistence mechanism that the attacker installed on affected hosts
Isolating a host from the network so that it can no longer reach any of the other systems
Writing the lessons-learned report for the leadership team after the incident has closed
Calling the affected customers to announce that the incident began and what it involved

explanation: Eradication removes the attacker's foothold, including persistence and malicious files. Isolation is containment, the lessons-learned report is post-incident activity, and customer announcements are escalation and communication.

stem: A responder confirms that an outside address downloaded the payroll files of current employees from a file server. What is the most appropriate next communication step?

options.text: Wait to report anything to leadership or counsel until the full investigation is closed
Escalate to senior leadership and legal counsel using the communication plan
Post the details on public social media to warn other organizations
Delete the copied records from the server to prevent more exposure

explanation: A confirmed data exposure is escalated internally right away, following the plan, so legal obligations can be assessed. Waiting delays notification deadlines, public posting skips legal review, and deleting records destroys evidence.

stem: Logs from servers in three time zones record events in local time. What should the analyst do before building an incident timeline?

options.text: Sort the events by the order in which each log file was received
Keep each source in its own time zone and compare by eye
Convert every timestamp to one reference time such as UTC
Remove the events that were logged outside business hours

explanation: A timeline only works when every event uses the same clock reference, and UTC is the usual choice. Sorting by file arrival or comparing mixed zones by eye produces wrong order, and dropping off-hours events removes likely attacker activity.

stem: Alert A shows adware pop-ups on one reception kiosk. Alert B shows a database server holding payment records beaconing to an unknown external host. How should the analyst triage them?

options.text: Handle A first because it was raised earlier in the shift and is already in the queue
Handle both at once by assigning the same priority to each and splitting the team evenly
Close A and B as low risk until more alerts arrive
Handle B first because of the data sensitivity and likely business impact

explanation: Triage orders work by impact and asset value, and payment data on a possibly compromised server outranks adware on a kiosk. Arrival order, equal priority and waiting for more alerts all ignore the risk difference.

stem: An EDR console shows that ws-0412.example.internal is running a credential theft tool. The analyst wants to stop lateral movement while keeping memory intact for analysis. Which action is best?

options.text: Use the EDR network isolation feature and leave the host powered on
Power the workstation off at the wall socket right away to end the activity
Reimage the workstation and restore the user files from backup
Disable only the user's mailbox and let the host keep running

explanation: EDR isolation cuts the host off from the network but keeps it running, so memory and processes remain available. Powering off loses volatile data, reimaging destroys evidence before analysis, and a mailbox change does not stop the host.

stem: Several servers show signs of compromise. The team moves them to a separate, tightly controlled zone that only the forensic tools can reach. Which containment technique is this?

options.text: Sinkholing of lookups for malicious domains
Segmentation into a quarantine network
Credential rotation for the affected service accounts
Application allow listing on the affected servers

explanation: Moving hosts into a restricted segment is segmentation, often called quarantine. Sinkholing redirects DNS lookups, credential rotation replaces secrets, and allow listing controls which programs may run.

stem: Many workstations are querying a known malicious domain. Which technique redirects those lookups to a controlled address so the infected hosts can be located?

options.text: Blocking the domain by IP address at the perimeter only
Adding the domain to the browser favorites policy
Creating a DNS sinkhole for the domain
Disabling DHCP on the affected subnet

explanation: A DNS sinkhole answers the lookup with a harmless address and reveals which hosts asked for it. An IP block at the perimeter shows nothing about internal clients, and the browser policy and DHCP change do not redirect lookups.

stem: A service account is seen signing in from an unusual host. The team wants to stop its use but keep its configuration for the investigation. What should they do?

options.text: Delete the account and its history, then recreate it under a new name
Change the password and leave existing sessions running
Move the account into the domain administrators group
Disable the account and revoke its active sessions and tokens

explanation: Disabling keeps the object and its history for investigation, and revoking sessions and tokens ends access already granted. Deleting loses evidence, a password change alone leaves live sessions, and adding administrator rights increases risk.

stem: Why does an examiner attach a write blocker when imaging a suspect drive?

options.text: To prevent any change to the original media during acquisition
To speed up the copy by skipping unused disk sectors on the original drive
To encrypt the image so that the suspect cannot read it
To remove deleted files before the image is hashed

explanation: A write blocker allows reads only, so the original stays unaltered and the evidence remains defensible. It does not speed up copying, encrypt the image or remove deleted data.

stem: Which reason best supports capturing memory from a compromised host before powering it down?

options.text: Memory images are much smaller than disk images, which makes them far easier to hash and to store
Running processes, live connections and keys sit only in volatile storage and vanish as soon as the power is switched off
Powering down a host makes most malware erase itself together with every trace of its own activity
Memory capture is a required first step before any compromised host can be reimaged or rebuilt

explanation: Volatile artifacts such as processes, connections and in-memory keys vanish when power is lost. Size is not the reason, malware does not reliably erase itself on shutdown, and no rule makes memory capture a prerequisite for reimaging.

stem: After malware is removed from a server, which step best helps confirm the attacker has not kept access?

options.text: Restart the server a few times and see whether the original alert reappears in the console
Delete the logs on the server so that old alerts stop appearing in the monitoring console
Reset the credentials exposed on the host and hunt for persistence on related systems
Add the server to a weekly report of healthy hosts that is sent to the management team

explanation: Exposed credentials let an attacker return, and related systems may hold other footholds, so both need checking. A restart proves little, deleting logs destroys evidence, and a status report does not test for access.

stem: Analysis shows a server has a kernel-level rootkit. Which eradication approach is most reliable?

options.text: Run a single antivirus scan from inside the running system and then return the server to service
Delete the files that the scan flags and keep the operating system
Disable the host firewall so the rootkit cannot hide its traffic
Rebuild the server from a known-good image and restore data only after scanning it

explanation: A rootkit can hide from tools running on the infected system, so rebuilding from a trusted image is the reliable fix. Scanning from inside the system and deleting flagged files can miss components, and disabling the firewall only adds exposure.

stem: Which factor most often decides whether regulators must be notified about a security incident?

options.text: Legal or contractual notification thresholds tied to the kind of data exposed
The number of alerts the SIEM raised during the incident, regardless of what they mean
The time of day at which the incident was first detected
Whether the attacker used a publicly known tool

explanation: Notification duties come from laws and contracts that depend on the data type and the extent of exposure. Alert volume, detection time and the attacker's tooling do not set those obligations.

stem: After recovery from an incident, a team raises logging detail and adds detection rules for the observed behavior. What is the main goal?

options.text: To reduce the storage cost of keeping detailed logs for long periods
To spot a repeat attempt or a missed foothold quickly
To replace the need for a lessons-learned review
To remove the need for vulnerability scanning

explanation: Continuous monitoring after recovery is aimed at catching reoccurrence or footholds that eradication missed. More logging raises storage use, and it neither replaces the review nor substitutes for scanning.

stem: Which finding is the strongest sign that an incident is wider than the first host that alerted?

options.text: The first host's alert was marked high severity by the detection rule that fired
The first host belongs to a user in the finance team
The same outbound destination appears in proxy logs for several other hosts
The first host has not been patched in several months

explanation: Other hosts contacting the same destination points to the same threat on more systems, which widens scope. Severity, the owner's department and patch age describe the first host only.

stem: A SIEM flags impossible travel for a user. The help desk confirms the user was on the company VPN whose exit point is in another country. How should the analyst classify the alert?

options.text: True positive, and begin containment of the user account and its active sessions right away
Informational, and delete the alert from the queue without any further note
Benign, and leave the rule unchanged so that it keeps firing on this pattern next time
False positive, with a note recorded and the rule tuned for that known egress address

explanation: The activity is explained and harmless, so it is a false positive, and documenting it plus tuning the rule prevents repeat noise. Treating it as a true positive wastes effort, and deleting or ignoring it leaves no record or improvement.

stem: Legal counsel tells the response team that litigation is likely. What must the team do with the relevant logs and forensic images?

options.text: Preserve them under a legal hold and suspend routine deletion until counsel releases them
Delete them once the incident is contained to limit liability
Share them with the affected vendor for safekeeping
Keep them only until the lessons-learned meeting has taken place

explanation: A legal hold requires keeping potentially relevant data until counsel releases it. Deleting it, handing it to a third party or keeping it for a short period risks spoliation and broken custody.

stem: The email system may itself be compromised during a major incident. What does a well-prepared communication plan provide for this case?

options.text: A single shared mailbox that every responder checks for new instructions
Pre-approved out-of-band channels and contact lists for responders
A rule that updates are sent only after the incident closes
A public status page that lists all technical details

explanation: The plan names alternative channels and contacts so responders can coordinate when normal tools cannot be trusted. A shared mailbox is the compromised channel, delayed updates fail stakeholders, and public technical details help the attacker.

stem: A production order server is compromised. Full isolation would stop all sales, and management wants the business to keep running. Which strategy best balances the need?

options.text: Leave the server untouched and keep watching it, expecting the attack to end by itself before any serious harm is done to orders or customers
Apply full isolation immediately without telling management, accepting that all sales will stop until the investigation is finished
Apply targeted containment, blocking attacker destinations and limiting lateral paths while monitoring, with stakeholder approval
Replace the server with a fresh one straight away and delete the old one at once, so that work can begin on a clean system

explanation: Targeted containment reduces attacker reach while keeping the service, and stakeholder approval records the accepted risk. Doing nothing lets harm continue, acting silently ignores the business impact, and deleting the old server destroys evidence.

stem: A responder has a running server with four evidence sources. Which order of collection follows the order of volatility?

options.text: Backup media, disk image, memory contents, CPU cache and registers
Disk image, CPU cache and registers, backup media, memory contents
Memory contents, CPU cache and registers, backup media, disk image
CPU cache and registers, memory contents, disk image, backup media

explanation: Order of volatility starts with the data that disappears fastest: CPU cache and registers, then memory contents, then the disk image, and finally backup media. Option a is the exact reverse, b collects the disk before the faster-changing sources, and c puts memory ahead of the cache and registers and takes backup media before the disk.

stem: The hash of an evidence image at transfer does not match the hash logged at acquisition. What does this imply for the case?

options.text: Integrity cannot be shown, so the mismatch is documented and the copy is not trusted until explained
The first hash was probably wrong, so the new value replaces it in the case record and the work continues
The mismatch is expected, because moving an image between systems changes its hash even when nothing in it has been altered
The image is fine as long as the file size is identical to the size that was recorded at acquisition

explanation: A changed hash means the content may differ, so the discrepancy must be recorded and the copy treated as unreliable until resolved. Replacing the recorded hash would erase the proof of the original state. A faithful copy produces the same hash, and matching file size does not prove identical content.

stem: A rebuilt file server is ready to return to production after ransomware. Which action best verifies that eradication succeeded?

options.text: Check that the rebuilt server responds to a ping from the management network and stays reachable
Scan the rebuilt server, compare it against its baseline, and place it under close monitoring for several weeks
Confirm the backup job ran before the incident began
Ask the owner whether files appear to open normally

explanation: Comparing against a baseline and monitoring closely tests for leftover changes and catches reinfection early. A ping shows only that the host is on, a backup job proves nothing about the rebuilt state, and user impressions miss hidden persistence.

stem:
Review the log excerpt.

```
2026-03-02T08:14:09Z vpn01 login ok user=mlopez src=203.0.113.50
2026-03-02T08:21:44Z fs02 session user=mlopez src=10.20.4.31
2026-03-02T09:02:17Z fs02 file reads=4120 user=mlopez
2026-03-02T09:05:31Z proxy01 upload dst=upload.example.net bytes=612000000 src=10.20.4.31
```

If the account is believed stolen and the transfer is still running, which action should come first?

options.text: Reboot `fs02` so that the open session and the transfer are cleared
Email the user to ask whether the upload was intended and wait for the reply
Block the upload destination and disable the account and its VPN session
Wait for the upload to finish so that the total size is known

explanation: Cutting off the destination and the stolen account stops further loss while keeping evidence on `fs02`. Rebooting `fs02` loses volatile data, emailing the account owner and waiting gives the attacker time while the account stays active, and waiting for the upload on `proxy01` to finish lets more data leave.

stem: An incident involves a vendor's remote access account on the network. Which escalation action is most appropriate under typical service contracts?

options.text: Post the vendor's name in the company chat so that staff know to avoid contact with that vendor entirely
Terminate the contract by email today and stop all communication with the vendor until legal replies
Wait for the vendor to discover the problem on its own and report it to the company later this week
Notify the vendor through its security contact and coordinate revoking the account's credentials

explanation: Contracts normally name a security contact, and joint action revokes access and gathers vendor logs. Naming the vendor in chat, ending the contract by email or waiting leaves the access path open or damages cooperation.

stem: During an active intrusion, a junior analyst proposes removing the one known malware file immediately. Why might the lead delay eradication?

options.text: A partial cleanup may tip off the attacker while other persistence remains elsewhere on the network
Malware files cannot be deleted while the host is running, so removal must wait for a planned shutdown
Eradication has to wait until the lessons-learned meeting has been held with the whole response team and management
The malware file is still needed to restore the host from backup after the intrusion has ended

explanation: Until scope is understood, a partial cleanup can tip off the attacker and miss other persistence. Files can be removed on a running host, eradication does not wait for the review meeting, and malware is not needed for restoration.

stem: Which TWO actions are containment techniques?

options.text: Isolating the affected host from the network
Reimaging the host from a trusted image
Disabling the compromised user account
Writing the lessons-learned report
Recomputing the hash of the memory image

explanation: Isolating the host and disabling the account both limit the attacker's reach right away. Reimaging is eradication, the report is post-incident work, and recomputing a hash is evidence validation.

stem: Which TWO details belong on a chain of custody form for a seized laptop?

options.text: The analyst's opinion on the attacker's motive
A unique evidence identifier and description of the laptop
The estimated cost of the incident to the business
Each person who took possession, with the date and time
The firewall rules that were changed during the incident

explanation: The form identifies the item and records every handoff with date and time. Motive, cost and firewall changes belong in other incident documents.

stem: Which TWO evidence sources are volatile?

options.text: The contents of memory
Files on an offline archive disk
Active network connections on the host
Backup tapes in a locked cabinet
Printed access logs filed in a binder

explanation: Memory and live connection state disappear when the host loses power or restarts. Archive disks, backup tapes and printed logs persist without power.

stem: Which THREE activities are part of eradication?

options.text: Removing malware and its persistence mechanisms
Capturing a memory image of the host
Patching the vulnerability that was exploited
Notifying regulators about the exposure
Resetting the credentials exposed on the host
Returning the service to users

explanation: Removing malware, closing the exploited weakness and resetting exposed credentials all take away the attacker's access. Memory capture is evidence acquisition, notification is escalation, and returning service is recovery.

stem: Which TWO factors should raise the priority of an incident during triage?

options.text: The alert arrived outside business hours
The affected asset supports a business-critical service
The ticket was opened by a senior manager
The data on the affected system is highly sensitive
The alert was created by the newest detection rule

explanation: Business criticality and data sensitivity measure impact, which drives priority. Arrival time, requester seniority and rule age say little about harm.

stem: Which TWO findings help determine the scope of an incident?

options.text: The age of the ticket in the queue
An EDR search showing the same malicious file hash on other hosts
The color of the severity label in the dashboard
Authentication logs showing the compromised account used on other systems
The name of the analyst who closed the previous ticket

explanation: Matching indicators on other hosts and use of the stolen account elsewhere show how far the attacker reached. Ticket age, label color and prior ticket handlers describe the queue, not the intrusion.

stem: Which TWO are internal escalation targets for a serious breach?

options.text: Law enforcement agencies
Legal counsel
Regulators
Senior leadership
Affected customers

explanation: Legal counsel and senior leadership are inside the organization and are notified first to guide decisions. Law enforcement, regulators and customers are external parties, usually contacted after internal review.

stem: Which THREE items should be recorded in incident documentation during the response?

options.text: A timeline of actions taken, using UTC
Guesses about which person is behind the attack
The commands run and the output they produced
Decisions made and who approved them
Opinions about how well colleagues performed
The full history of unrelated tickets

explanation: A UTC timeline, commands with output and approved decisions give a reliable, reviewable record. Speculation, personal opinions and unrelated tickets add noise and can weaken the record.

stem: Which TWO are valid reasons to delay eradication during an active incident?

options.text: The scope is not yet known and early removal could tip off the attacker
The backup copies are encrypted with a key that only the backup administrator holds
Users and managers have asked for the service to be restored as quickly as possible today, before the end of the week
Law enforcement has asked the organization to preserve the situation for a short time
The next routine status meeting with the management team is two days away from the day of the incident

explanation: Unknown scope and a law enforcement request are sound reasons to hold off. Backup encryption, user pressure and a distant status meeting affect recovery planning rather than justify leaving the attacker in place.

stem: Which THREE steps help verify a restored system before it returns to production?

options.text: Searching its logs for any activity from known attacker addresses
Deleting its logs to save disk space
Confirming that the exploited weakness is patched
Disabling the endpoint agent to speed up boot
Reusing the old administrator credentials for convenience
Checking that restored data came from a known-good backup

explanation: Log review for attacker activity, patch confirmation and a trusted backup source all reduce the chance of reinfection. Deleting logs, disabling the agent and reusing old credentials weaken detection and security.

stem: Which TWO practices are correct when handling a forensic disk image?

options.text: Analyze the original drive directly to avoid copy errors
Hash the original and the copy and record both values
Store the only copy on a shared analyst desktop
Work from a copy and keep the original sealed in access-controlled storage
Rename files inside the image to make them easier to read

explanation: Hashing both and working from a copy with the original secured preserve integrity and custody. Working on the original, using a shared desktop and renaming files all risk altering or losing the evidence.

stem: Host web03.example.internal is suspected of beaconing to an attacker. Review the connection list, then complete each step.

output: Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port   Process

steps.label: Type a command that shows the executable that process ID 3918 is running from

options.text: Isolate web03 from the network but leave it powered on
Power web03 off immediately to stop the connection
Delete the updsvc file and restart the service
Stop the sshd service so that no one can sign in

steps.label: Choose what to collect before anyone reboots or changes the host

options.text: A memory image and the list of running processes
A fresh copy of last week's backup
The help desk ticket history for the host
The hardware inventory record for the host

explanation: The `/proc` entry for a process ID links to its executable, which shows where `updsvc` really runs from. Isolating the host stops the beaconing while keeping memory available, and memory and process state are the most volatile evidence to capture before any reboot. Powering off, deleting the file or stopping `sshd` would either lose evidence or miss the attacker connection.

partExplanations.path: The exe link under `/proc/3918` shows the program path for that process ID.
partExplanations.contain: Isolation cuts the attacker link while the host stays on, so memory and processes are preserved.
partExplanations.next: Memory and running process state are the most volatile and are lost at reboot.

stem: A server shows signs of a stolen account. Review the authentication log excerpt, then complete each step.

output: Mar  2 08:14:02 app07 sshd[2210]: Failed password for deploy from 198.51.100.23 port 40122 ssh2
Mar  2 08:14:05 app07 sshd[2212]: Failed password for deploy from 198.51.100.23 port 40130 ssh2
Mar  2 08:14:09 app07 sshd[2214]: Failed password for deploy from 198.51.100.23 port 40144 ssh2
Mar  2 08:14:15 app07 sshd[2216]: Accepted password for deploy from 198.51.100.23 port 40152 ssh2
Mar  2 08:19:40 app07 sudo: deploy : cmd=/usr/bin/tar czf /tmp/export.tgz /srv/customers
Mar  2 08:21:02 app07 sshd[2230]: Connection closed by 198.51.100.23 port 40152

steps.label: Type a command that shows only the lines in /var/log/auth.log that contain the word Accepted
Choose the best action for the deploy account

options.text: Disable the account and end its active sessions, keeping its settings
Delete the account and its home directory
Reboot app07 so that the account signs out
Leave the account enabled and watch for a second login

steps.label: Choose the best next communication step for the archive of customer records

options.text: Brief legal counsel and senior leadership following the communication plan
Close the ticket as a false positive because the login succeeded
Email affected customers directly before legal review
Delete /tmp/export.tgz at once to remove the exposure

explanation: Filtering for Accepted shows the successful login that followed repeated failures. Disabling the account stops the attacker while keeping the account for investigation, and an archive of customer records staged for transfer out is escalated to legal and leadership. Emailing customers before legal review skips the notification rules and approvals. Deleting the account or archive destroys evidence, a reboot leaves the credential usable, and a successful login does not make the activity benign.

partExplanations.find: `grep` prints only the lines that contain Accepted, which isolates the successful sign-in.
partExplanations.account: Disabling and ending sessions blocks the attacker and preserves the account for the investigation.
partExplanations.escalate: Staged customer data raises legal obligations, so legal and leadership are told first.

sudo dd of=/evidence/ws0412.img if=/dev/sdb status=* bs=* conv=*
sudo dd if=/dev/sdb of=/evidence/ws0412.img status=* conv=*
sudo dd of=/evidence/ws0412.img if=/dev/sdb status=* conv=*
sudo dd if=/dev/sdb of=/evidence/ws0412.img status=* conv=* bs=*
sudo dd of=/evidence/ws0412.img if=/dev/sdb status=* conv=* bs=*

explanation: A write blocker lets the examiner read the original without altering it. `dd` copies the whole device bit for bit to an image file, and a SHA-256 hash from `sha256sum` recorded at acquisition lets anyone later show the image is unchanged. Speed, encryption and wiping deleted files are not what a write blocker does.

partExplanations.why: The blocker allows reads only, so the original evidence stays unaltered.
partExplanations.image: `dd` with `if` set to the source device and `of` set to the image file makes a bit-for-bit copy.
partExplanations.hash: The hash taken at acquisition is the baseline for later integrity checks.

stem: Ransomware activity is confirmed on ws-0412.example.internal. Configure the EDR containment policy for this host.

options.text: Isolate the host, keeping the EDR and responder connections only
Monitor only, with no network restriction
Block DNS lookups but allow all other traffic
End active sessions and lock the signed-in account
Leave sessions open so the user can save work
Sign the user out and allow an immediate new sign-in
Keep the host powered on so memory can be captured
Shut the host down to stop the encryption
Put the host to sleep until the morning

fields.label: Mapped network shares used by the host

options.text: Revoke the host's access to the shares and check them for changes
Keep the shares mapped so the files stay available
Leave access as is and trust the file server backups

explanation: Isolation with only the EDR and responder paths open stops spread while analysts keep control. Locking the account removes the active user session, staying powered on preserves memory, and revoking share access protects other systems while their files are checked for changes.

partExplanations.mode: Isolation with a narrow allow list stops spread but keeps the response tools working.
partExplanations.sessions: Ending sessions and locking the account removes the active user session from the host.
partExplanations.power: Memory holds volatile evidence that a shutdown would destroy.
partExplanations.shares: Ransomware can encrypt files on any share the host can reach, so access is cut and the shares are checked.

stem: Legal counsel expects a dispute over the web03 incident. Configure how the case evidence is retained and handled.

fields.label: Retention of incident logs and images

options.text: Hold until the case is closed and counsel releases them
Keep for the standard 30-day log cycle and then let the normal rotation delete them
Purge after the incident report is written and the lessons-learned review is held
A restricted evidence store with access logging
A shared analyst folder on the main file server that the whole team can open
Email attachments sent to every member of the case team and to the lawyers
At acquisition and at every transfer or access
Once, when the case is closed and the final report has been signed off
Only if the image is shared with someone outside the company or sent to a vendor
Named responders, each entry recorded in the custody log
Any member of the security team, with no record of who took the evidence
Any employee who asks for it, as long as their manager agrees to the request

explanation: A legal hold overrides routine deletion, a restricted store with logging protects the images, hashes at each handoff prove they are unchanged, and a custody log of named handlers keeps the evidence defensible.

partExplanations.retention: A legal hold keeps the data until counsel releases it, so routine cycles are suspended.
partExplanations.storage: A restricted, logged store limits access and records who touched the images.
partExplanations.integrity: A hash at acquisition and at each transfer shows no change between handoffs.
partExplanations.access: Named handlers with log entries keep the chain of custody unbroken.

stem: A workstation is infected and calling out to an attacker. Place the best containment technique for each need named below the network path.

zones.name: Keep the workstation off the rest of the internal network
Reveal which hosts look up the attacker domain
Stop traffic to the attacker address from any host
End use of the stolen user credentials

labels.text: Quarantine VLAN on the access switch port
Egress block rule for the attacker address
Disable the account and revoke sessions

explanation: Each need maps to a containment technique: a quarantine VLAN limits lateral reach, a sinkhole shows which clients query the domain, an egress block cuts the address for every host, and disabling the account ends the stolen credentials. Reimaging is eradication and restoring from backup is recovery, so neither fits a containment need.

partExplanations.z1: A quarantine VLAN keeps the host from reaching internal systems.
partExplanations.z2: A sinkhole answers the lookup with a controlled address and exposes the clients that ask.
partExplanations.z3: An egress rule at the perimeter blocks that address for every internal host.
partExplanations.z4: Disabling the account and revoking sessions removes the stolen access.

stem: Sources log in different time zones. Use the table to normalize times to UTC and answer each question.

payload.caption: Events for the dnguyen account on 9 March (times as logged)

fields.label: UTC time the bulk file read starts
Minutes from the VPN login to the start of the upload
Minutes from the start of the upload to the alert

explanation: Convert each time to UTC by subtracting the offset. `fs05` is UTC-5, so 08:20 becomes 13:20 UTC. `proxy02` is UTC+1, so 14:41 becomes 13:41 UTC.

partExplanations.read: 08:20 at an offset of -5 is 08:20 + 5 hours = 13:20 UTC.
partExplanations.gap: Upload 14:41 at +1 is 13:41 UTC; 13:41 minus the 13:02 login is 39 minutes.
partExplanations.alert: Upload at 13:41 UTC and alert at 13:55 UTC are 14 minutes apart.
